newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican governor says drug lords out to get him.
newsitem.headline: Mexican governor says drug lords out to get him.

text.p: The embattled governor of a Mexican border state says recent accusations by U.S. government agencies linking him to the narcotics trade were probably cooked up by Mexican drug lords seeking revenge for his anti-drug efforts.

In an interview with Reuters, Sonora state Gov. Manlio Fabio Beltrones firmly denied reports he has allowed Mexico's most notorious drug kingpin to set up a major trafficking operation in his state, which shares a 300-mile-long (500 km) border with the United States.

"It is false and absurd ... It is a perverse game by those who have been hurt by my frontal attack against narcotrafficking," said Beltrones, 44, an influential member of Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

The popular governor has been dogged by scandal since February, when a New York Times report alleged he had protected Amado Carrillo Fuentes, head of the powerful Juarez cartel and a man U.S. officials badly want to see locked up. The article quoted unnamed U.S. officials and intelligence.

The affair has raised questions about the extent to which Mexico's leading politicians have been corrupted by the multibillion-dollar drug trade and hurt relations between the world's largest drug consumer and its neighbour.

During the two-hour interview, one of his first since the scandal broke, Beltrones painted himself as the victim of drug cartels and not their political patron, and as a man who in six years in office had successfully prevented neighbouring cartels from setting up shop in Sonora. His term ends in October.

Mexico's second biggest state in size, Sonora's rugged and remote desert is an ideal spot to ferry cocaine, marijuana and methamphetamines north to Arizona. The state is hemmed in on either side by Carrillo's Juarez cartel in neighbouring Chihuahua and the Arrellano Felix drug gang in nearby Tijuana.

"It is possible this information was given (to U.S. intelligence) by my enemies ... (as) revenge for my efforts to prevent them from setting up in Sonora," he said, adding he had received death threats from unspecified cartel leaders.

Once considered a rising star within Mexico's PRI and a protege to former Mexican President Carlos Salinas, Beltrones lashed out at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency for leaking information that he said was based on raw gossip, not facts.

The United States has so far not filed any formal charges against Beltrones. A senior U.S. diplomat told Reuters a multi-agency committee recently found there was not enough evidence against Beltrones to strip his rights to a U.S. visa -- something denied regularly to suspected drug traffickers.

There is little doubt the drug trade has mushroomed in past years in northern Mexico. DEA director Thomas Constantine testified to Congress last year that Mexican cartels had eclipsed their Colombian counterparts in size and muscle.

During Beltrones' term, which began in 1991, Carrillo Fuentes' power rose, gaining him the nickname "Lord of the Skies" for his ability to fly cocaine-laden planes undetected from South America to Mexico.

Business was so good that cartel leaders became increasingly brash. Carrillo owned a pink stucco home just blocks from the U.S. consul's home in a posh Hermosillo district and was finishing an opulent, moorish-style mansion a few blocks from the governor's mansion when Beltrones took power and ordered it seized.

Many in Sonora doubt Beltrones is directly linked to the drugs trade and his approval ratings have risen since the affair. Beltrones' hand-picked successor, Armando Lopez Nogales, is also leading in polls ahead of the July 6 gubernatorial race.
